FDA recalls franko herbal mixture, shuts down Ashanti factory over drug adulteration
Ghana's FDA has ordered a recall of Franko Herbal Mixture and shut down its Ashanti factory after detecting diazepam and paracetamol in the product.
Advertisement
The FDA has ordered Franko Herbal Centre to recall its Franko Herbal Mixture within 14 days and shut down its Jacobu factory after detecting diazepam and paracetamol in the product.
The Authority warns that the substances pose health risks, including respiratory depression, coma, death and severe liver damage.
The FDA has warned of further sanctions, including criminal prosecution, for non-compliance and urged the public to stop using the product and report sellers.
Advertisement
Advertisement
The
Food and Drugs Authority (FDA)
has ordered Franko Herbal Centre to recall its Franko Herbal Mixture from the market within 14 days after laboratory tests detected diazepam and paracetamol in the product.
In a notice dated October 19, 2026, the Authority also announced the closure of the company's manufacturing factory at Jacobu in the Ashanti Region, warning that failure to comply with the directives could lead to further regulatory sanctions, including criminal prosecution.
The FDA said it would oversee the safe disposal of the recalled products and urged the public to stop purchasing and consuming the herbal mixture because of the potential health risks associated with the substances detected.

Advertisement
Advertisement
According to the Authority, laboratory analysis established that Franko Herbal Mixture, which was registered as a herbal medicinal product containing Carica papaya, Alstonia boonei and Tetrapleura tetraptera, had been adulterated with diazepam and paracetamol.
Diazepam is a prescription-only medicine belonging to the benzodiazepine class. It is used to treat conditions including anxiety disorders, acute alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasms and certain types of seizures.
The
FDA warned
that diazepam can interact with other medicines, potentially increasing the risk of severe sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death.
It added that long-term use or abuse of the medicine can affect the central nervous system, with possible symptoms including confusion, forgetfulness, dizziness, fatigue, nightmares, hallucinations, impaired judgement and seizures.
READ ALSO:
5 foods that may slow ageing and keep you looking younger
Advertisement
Advertisement
Paracetamol, meanwhile, is a medicine commonly used to relieve mild-to-moderate pain and reduce fever. The Authority warned that an overdose can cause severe liver damage and acute liver failure, which can be fatal if not treated promptly.
The FDA said the presence of the two pharmaceutical substances in a product registered as herbal medicine posed serious health and safety risks to consumers.
The Authority said the adulteration of herbal medicinal products is an offence under Section 111 of the Public Health Act, 2012 (Act 851), which prohibits the sale of adulterated herbal medicinal products.
It also noted that the law prohibits the manufacture, labelling, packaging, sale or advertisement of herbal medicinal products in ways that are false, misleading or deceptive about their character, quality, composition and other properties.
According to the FDA, Franko Herbal Mixture is registered as a herbal medicinal product and must not contain other drug substances.
Advertisement
Advertisement
The Authority has directed the company to withdraw the product from the market within 14 days and warned that failure to comply could result in additional sanctions, including criminal prosecution.

The FDA has also urged retailers and distributors to comply with the recall directive and called on members of the public to report anyone selling Franko Herbal Mixture to the nearest FDA office.
It reiterated its
warning that consumers should refrain from buying or using the product.

news_title: FDA gives Franko Herbal Centre 14 days to recall diazepam-tainted mixture - Graphic Online
efet_title: FDA gives Franko Herbal Centre 14 days to recall diazepam-tainted mixture - Graphic Online
efet_body:
Featured
FDA gives Franko Herbal Centre 14 days to recall diazepam-tainted mixture
Mohammed Ali
Oct - 20 - 2026 , 13:06
2 minutes read
The Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) has given Franko Herbal Centre 14 days to recall Franko Herbal Mixture from the market after the FDA said laboratory tests found the product contained diazepam and paracetamol, which were not declared as ingredients.
In a product recall notice signed by the Chief Executive Officer and dated October 19, 2026, the FDA directed the public, retailers and distributors to report anyone still selling the mixture to the nearest FDA office.
The Authority said the manufacturing factory at Jacobu in the Ashanti Region had been closed down. It added that the recalled products would be safely disposed of.
It warned Franko Herbal Centre that failure to comply with the directives could attract further regulatory sanctions, including criminal prosecution.
The FDA said the action followed laboratory analysis of Franko Herbal Mixture, manufactured by Franko Herbal Centre at Jacobu. The product was registered as containing three herbal plants, Carica papaya, Alstonia boonei and Tetrapleura tetraptera.
The analysis, however, established that the mixture had been adulterated with diazepam and paracetamol.
The Authority advised the public against purchasing or consuming the product. It also urged retailers and distributors to comply with the recall directive and report anyone offering the mixture for sale to help remove it from the market.
The FDA described diazepam as a benzodiazepine and a prescription-only medicine used to treat anxiety disorders, acute alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasms and certain types of seizures.
It said paracetamol was an over-the-counter medicine used to relieve mild-to-moderate pain and fever.
According to the Authority, the presence of the two drugs in a herbal medicinal product poses serious health risks.
It explained that diazepam could interact with other medicines and increase the risk of severe sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death.
Long-term use or abuse of the drug could also affect the central nervous system, causing confusion, forgetfulness, dizziness, fatigue, nightmares, hallucinations, impaired judgement and seizures, the FDA said.
On paracetamol, the Authority warned that an overdose could cause severe liver damage and acute liver failure, which could be fatal without prompt treatment.
The FDA said the adulteration of herbal medicinal products was an offence under Section 111 of the Public Health Act, 2012 (Act 851), which prohibits the sale of adulterated herbal medicinal products.
It added that the law also prohibited the manufacture, labelling, packaging, sale or advertisement of herbal medicinal products in ways that were false, misleading or deceptive about their character, nature, quality, substance or composition.
The Authority stated that Franko Herbal Mixture “flouts all these requirements and more”.
It explained that the product was registered as a herbal medicinal product and, therefore, must not contain any other drug substance.

Maureen Lartey (with mic) addressing traders at the Mallam Atta Market in Accra
THE Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) has intensified food safety education among traders and food handlers at the Mallam Atta Market in Accra to address food contamination and the misuse of chemicals in food production and handling.
The initiative is part of the authority's activities to mark World Food Safety Day, observed annually on June 7, and aims to promote safe food-handling practices and reduce food-borne illnesses.
Speaking at an engagement with traders at the market in Accra on Friday, on the theme, “From Burden to Solution: Safe Food Everywhere,” the Director of Food Safety and Consumer Education at the FDA, Maureen Lartey, said the authority was continuing its public education efforts, particularly in the informal sector, where food safety concerns persisted.
She said the authority selected the market for the engagement after reporting a 100 per cent pass rate in screenings for Sudan dyes in palm oil in 2025.
Lartey said the FDA had worked with local assemblies and their environmental health officers to educate traders on safe food-handling practices and the importance of maintaining hygienic conditions.
She said although sustained public education had led to progress over the years, more needed to be done to improve compliance with food safety standards.
She identified food adulteration, including adding flour and coconut oil to peanut butter and the presence of yeast in corn and cassava dough, as concerns the authority was addressing.
According to her, the FDA was intensifying its efforts to educate traders and food handlers about such practices to protect consumers from potentially harmful products.
Lartey urged traders and consumers to buy food from safe, reliable sources, warning that some produce could contain high levels of pesticide residues because farmers misuse chemicals.
She cautioned traders to be careful when sourcing food for sale, especially from farmers known to misuse agrochemicals.
